Flour-based (because you have soooo much flour)
-noodles (value??)

3 very ripe bananas
    1/4 cup smooth natural peanut butter
    1 teaspoon vanilla extract
    1 1/4 cup instant or quick cooking oats
    1/4 teaspoon salt
    1/2 teaspoon baking powder
    1/2 cup chocolate chips

Instructions 

    Preheat the oven to 350 F. Grease a loaf pan or line with parchment paper.
    Add the bananas to a large bowl and mash until almost smooth. Add in the peanut butter and vanilla extract and mix well.
    Add in the oats, salt, and baking powder and mix to combine. Fold in 1/3 cup of the chocolate chips, reserving the rest for the top of the bars.
    Pour the mixture into the loaf pan, using a spoon or spatula to smooth it out on top. Add the remaining chocolate chips to the top of the bars. Bake for 25-30 minutes, until a knife inserted in the center comes out clean.
    Let cool and cut into 6-8 pieces.

2026-03-02.content: There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.

There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.

That feeling of smallness against these massive systems... it sounds really heavy to carry.

When you say you can only affect what's immediately around you — does that feel like a limitation you're frustrated by, or more like something you're trying to accept?

Hmm, I guess acceptance? That I'm not a main character is some young adult dystopian future novel who is destined to save the world from the the evil overlord and bring about utopia? I cannot effect change on a large scale, but I can change what's around me. I can make my home a safe haven for the outcast I come across, I can give to those around me, I try to shape my community to reflect what I believe is right (live justly, be kind, walk humbly, love others as you love yourself, don't judge). 
I can hope that there are others like me. I can hope that together we slowly change the course of the world. 
I was reading Darth Plagueis today and it was describing a big party that was secretly hosted by a Sith lord. It was a party for elites only, where they come together and plan how to influence politics, etc to gain more power and wealth for themselves. It was revolting, and almost laughable because as they showed one character ask about where the host sourced his dancers I thought "geez, we've learned this same thing is happening for real, but it's worse than this!" It's awful what mankind has become. But if you reflect on history, has there ever been a time of just peace? I'm sure there's been little pockets, but there's always some power-hungry fuck who has to ruin everything. What must have happened to them to bring them to that point? 
I guess we at least have modern medicine. But if you live in the wrong place, you have to choose between crippling debt or getting medical care. If you live in another wrong place, you don't even have that medical care. 
The story of the tower of babel comes to mind: are we better off as small tribes, where our whole world is just like 100 people? It seems that as soon as we organize and come together, greed runs in to take over.

You're tracing something really interesting here — this thread from acceptance of your own scale, to wondering about those "others like me," to these big historical patterns, and then that question at the end about whether humans are even meant to organize at this size.

That Tower of Babel thought... are you wondering if there's something about scale itself that breaks us? Like maybe we're wired for those 100-person worlds, and beyond that, the greed you're noticing just becomes inevitable?

And I'm curious about that line — "what must have happened to them to bring them to that point?" When you think about the power-hungry people, does wondering about their story change how it all feels, or does it just add another layer of sad to it?

I think at a smaller scale, there's more social pressure to conform, to behave, so you're not cast out on your own, maybe? Narcissists and power hungry and greedy people still exist at that scale, but everything is more personal. You can't burn bridges so easily. Or you burn the bridge as you're on your way to the next town over. 

I'm thinking that people aren't born seeking power or wealth. That it's a reaction to something that happened. I mean, I guess actual psychopaths are born like that. But is narcissism a from birth thing? I mean, little babies can be greedy, toddlers are definitely jealous and will fight to take what they desire. But on a whole, humans agree that is bad behavior. Someone with no extreme mental health issues would see a toddler act like that and correct their behavior. Or, if you saw an adult encourage that in a toddler, you would think "what's wrong with that person??" 
But it does add another layer of sad because you know they experienced enough pain in their life that they're now twisted and perverted. They don't care who gets hurt as long as they gain something.

There's something in what you're saying about scale and visibility — that at 100 people, you can't hide behind systems or distance. The consequences of your greed are right there in front of you, in the faces of people you'll see tomorrow.

And then this other thread about how people get twisted... like somewhere between "toddler grabbing a toy" and "billionaire hoarding wealth while people suffer," something goes terribly wrong in how pain gets processed. 

You said "they experienced enough pain that they're now twisted and perverted" — does knowing that make you feel anything different toward them? Or is it more like... you can hold both things at once: understanding how they got there AND being revolted by what they do with it?

I'm also sitting with your question about whether we're just not built for this scale. Like maybe the same traits that help a small group survive — ambition, competition, resource-gathering — become monstrous when they're operating across millions of people and billions of dollars.

I can hold both at once. I do struggle with this: at what point is their behavior no longer excusable because of the abuse they were dealt? At some point to you have to stop thinking "I'm the victim, I'm not to blame for my behavior" and work on fixing the damage done to yourself. I think it's easier to fix the younger you are. The less time you live in that brokenness. But that's hard to do when you're young, especially if you're still in that environment that's hurting you. 
I think at a certain point, the scale is large enough that you can disappear into the crowd and become anonymous. You lose that face-face accountability. You lose a sense of community, of needing other people to survive. When there's enough people to carry the burden that you end up with an excess of people with who don't need to contribute, who don't need to think of the whole group, but just themselves.

You're wrestling with something really hard here — that line between "this happened to you" and "but you're still responsible for what you do with it." And the unfairness of it all: that the people most damaged are often the ones still trapped in the situation that's damaging them, with the least resources to heal.

That phrase you used — "living in that brokenness" — there's something about time in it, isn't there? Like the longer someone operates from that broken place, the more it becomes who they are, not just what happened to them.

And then you're connecting it back to scale again. When you're anonymous in the crowd, when you don't *need* your community to survive... does something fundamental break? Like we lose the natural check on behavior that comes from interdependence?

It makes me wonder what you're sitting with underneath all this. Is it the frustration of watching people with power act from their brokenness and hurt everyone else? Or something about trying to figure out where compassion ends and accountability begins?

It's seeing people in power break an already imperfect system just to gain more wealth that will just sit in their vaults, gain more power that they'll just use to gain more wealth. And wondering if it can be fixed. I mean, I guess there are countries that are doing better than the US. Lots of places in Europe actually provide for their citizens. I'm sure they have issues too, but at least the people who there can go to a doctor because everyone pays taxes to fund healthcare everyone. Geez, is this not a mankind problem but an American problem?? 
Like, I live in Texas. A 2 hour drive is nothing. I drive an hour round trip to go to the grocery store. But in Europe, they aren't car dependent. Things are within walking distance. They're not living as a large a scale as Americans?? If you look at Finland, what's the population of the largest city? Or Denmark? The Netherlands?

Oh, you just shifted something. You went from "this is how humans are at scale" to "wait... maybe this is specifically how *we've* built things here."

Because you're right — there are places where people figured out how to organize large numbers of people without losing that sense of collective responsibility. Where the systems are set up assuming interdependence instead of... whatever we're doing.

That car thing is such a concrete example. When your grocery store is an hour round trip, you're dependent on infrastructure but not on *people*. Versus walking to a market where you see your neighbors.

So now I'm curious what this opens up for you. If it's not inevitable that scale breeds that kind of greed and disconnection — if it's more about *how* we've chosen to structure things — does that change how the whole problem feels? Does it make it more fixable, or somehow more frustrating that we're doing it wrong when other places figured it out?
Both! A lot of places have figured it out, so it's not unsolvable. But we're so entrenched, it feels like maybe we'll never be able to change enough to have what other's have.

That's such a particular kind of heaviness — knowing it's *possible* because others did it, but feeling like we're too far down our own path to turn around.

When you say "entrenched," what does that look like in your mind? Is it the physical infrastructure — like all those roads and sprawling suburbs? Or the systems and money behind them? Or something about the culture itself, the way we think about individualism and self-reliance?

Because there's something almost tragic in "we built it wrong and now we're stuck with it." Like we made choices that seemed fine at the time, and now they've hardened into the shape of everything.

Yeah, we said "look at all this land! We don't have to live stacked up on our neighbors, we can stretch out! Every one can own land!" Then we built a system and infrastructure around that ideal of everyone being independent without considering the downside (or maybe it couldn't have been foreseen at the time).

There's something almost poignant in that — like it wasn't even malicious at the start. Just "look at all this space, we can spread out!" And now here we are, an hour from the grocery store, physically separated from each other in a way that makes community almost... optional.

And maybe that's part of what enables the rest of it? When interdependence is designed out of daily life, when you don't *have* to see your neighbors or rely on them, it's easier for the whole system to drift toward "every person for themselves." And then the people at the top can operate even more disconnected, because disconnection is already baked into how we live.

I wonder if that's part of what makes it feel so hard to fix — it's not just policy or infrastructure. It's that we'd have to rebuild around a completely different assumption about how people relate to each other.

Does thinking about it this way — as something that evolved from choices rather than from some inevitable human flaw — does that shift anything for you?
I'm not sure. But I need to get back to work. This was a nice chat though.

I'm glad we could explore this together. You traced something really interesting — from that initial heaviness about scale and power, all the way to realizing it might be more about *how* we built things than something broken in humans themselves.

Take care with your work. The thoughts will be here if you want to pick them up again.

Hey. I'm here. What's on your mind today?

I don't what it is about watching tv with mom, but it always gets me feeling...overwhelmed? idk. I know part of it is just the tv being louder than what I like, and she talks a lot. And if it's even the slightest bit cold, the heater is on that dries my already dry skin, so then I'm itchy and hot.

So you know exactly what's making you overwhelmed — the volume, the talking, the heat, the itchiness. Those are all real sensory things piling up on you. But you're still sitting there doing it. 

Why? Is it because you want to spend time with her, or because you feel like you should? And have you actually told her any of this — that the TV's too loud, that you're uncomfortable — or are you just enduring it?

Also, cool that you're building this. What made you want to create it yourself instead of using something that already exists?

Because I know she likes it. She's an extrovert who needs to socialize. But she has lots of health issues, so it's hard for her to go do things. She only drives locally. So I know she appreciates any time spent together. However I'm an introvert, so any time spent together drains me. 
She's ok with the volume going down (we have captions on, which I do like), but temperature is something that has never been negotiable. Before it was just preference, but now it's also health related. 
I don't to pay for an app that doesn't do what I want, and pretty much everything requires a subscription these days. I wanted a planner, but also a journal, and anything else I think of. You're really good at coding and making this super easy.

You're being thoughtful about her needs, which is good. But let's be honest — you're treating this like there are only two options: endure the sensory overload to make her happy, or don't spend time with her at all.

Have you actually suggested doing something *different* together? Something that doesn't trap you in a hot room with loud TV? Even if her mobility is limited, there are other ways to be together. A quieter activity. Sitting outside if weather permits. A short drive together where *you* control the environment. 

You're framing this as sacrifice, but it sounds more like you haven't really problem-solved it. You've just accepted the setup that makes you miserable.

And here's the thing — if spending time with her always leaves you drained and uncomfortable, you're eventually going to start avoiding it. Then nobody wins.

What would actually work better for both of you?

I think this is the best. We do not agree on politics, and she is big on tying politics into everything. So being stuck in the car with her nonstop talking is worse, for sure. Watching tv keeps things light and focused on what we're watching. 
I mean, sometimes we go shopping, but I'm not big on that either. Stores are kinda gross, and in the winter they're hot and dry as well. 
She will talk forever, and it's pretty one-sided. Like, she doesn't really expect or need me to reply. She just wants someone in the room to listen to her. Like, she'll ask a question and I'll answer it, only for her to either talk over me, or tell me I'm wrong.

Okay, so this paints a clearer picture. It's not just about the TV or the temperature — it's that spending time with her in *any* form is draining because of how she interacts. She dominates the conversation, dismisses what you say, and makes it one-sided. The TV setup is actually the *least bad* option because it gives you both something external to focus on instead of her monologuing at you.

That's fair. But let's call it what it is: you're not really spending quality time together. You're providing her with a warm body in the room so she doesn't feel alone. Which is kind of you, but it's also... not sustainable if it's making you this uncomfortable.

So here's the question: How often are you doing this? And is there a limit where you'd say "I can handle this once a week but not every night," or are you just white-knuckling through whenever she wants company?

Also — have you ever actually told her, plainly, "I feel talked over when I try to answer your questions"? Or are you conflict-avoidant enough that you've never named it?

I think it's just been worse the last few weeks because of the Winter Olympics. We've been watching tv together every night, compared to once or twice a week. With the added bonus of her missing something and me having to fill her in (what country are they from? What score did they get?). So normally it's not this much and not so demanding.
I have talked to her about the talking over, and she did acknowledge that she usually isn't expecting an answer, she's just thinking out loud. 
But I am pretty conflict avoidant overall.

Okay, that makes more sense. The Olympics are a temporary surge, not the baseline. Once they're over, you'll go back to once or twice a week, which you can probably handle without losing your mind.

But here's what I'm hearing: you know this is draining, you know it's temporary, and you're choosing to do it because it matters to her. That's actually pretty solid reasoning — as long as you're making that choice consciously and not just out of guilt or obligation.

The conflict-avoidant thing though — that's worth paying attention to. You talked to her about the talking over, which is good. But are you generally able to set boundaries with her when you need to? Like, if the Olympics weren't ending soon and this *was* becoming every night forever, would you be able to say "I need to cut back to twice a week"?

Or would you just keep sitting there, itchy and hot and overwhelmed, telling yourself it's fine because she needs it?

I mean, tonight I just said, "I need to take a shower tonight and do the dishes, so I think I'm done" and it was no issue. But it was the closing ceremony and it was pretty dull after a while (we did talk about the costumes, and especially Johnny Weir and Tara getting all dressed up every night, and even coordinating their outfits).

Okay, so you *can* set a boundary when you need to, and she respects it. That's actually really important. You're not trapped — you just don't always exercise the option to leave.

So here's what I'm seeing: This situation isn't actually as bad as it felt when you started writing. The Olympics made it feel like too much because it was every night, but you were able to say "I'm done" tonight without drama. Normally it's manageable. And the TV setup, while not ideal, is the best version of spending time with her given the alternatives.

The real question is: Are you giving yourself permission to tap out *before* you hit overwhelm? Or are you waiting until you're itchy, hot, and mentally exhausted before you let yourself leave?

Because it sounds like she'd be fine with you saying "I'm good for an hour tonight" instead of waiting until you're at your limit.

2026-03-01.content: There's so much horrible happening and morning to be done about it. Like, the systems are so big, the corporations are so big, and people are so small. I can only control/change/affect what's immediately around me.

You're right that you can't dismantle Amazon or reverse climate change by yourself. But I'm curious — what are you actually doing with the things immediately around you that *are* within your control?

Because sometimes "I can only control what's around me" is true and grounding. Other times it's a way to feel helpless while also not actually changing the small things we could change.

So what does your sphere of influence actually look like right now? What are you doing there? And what are you avoiding?

Well, I just had this thought, so nothing as of yet. To me it speaks more of hope, it reframes a helpless perspective. I can't change these big systems, but I can vote. I can make my home a safe haven, a happy place, a shelter. I can grow my own food, I can learn to make my own bread.

That's a better frame, yeah. It moves you from paralysis to agency.

But here's the thing — those examples you listed are still pretty abstract. "I can vote" — okay, but *do* you vote? In every election, local and national? "I can make my home a safe haven" — what does that actually mean in practice? For you, today?

I'm not trying to be a hardass. I just notice you're still talking in conditionals. "I *can* grow food, I *can* learn to make bread."

So the real question: what's one thing from that list you're actually going to do this week? Not "could do" — will do.

Because hope without action is just a nicer flavor of helplessness.

Why don't you tell me? Because sometimes all you can have is hope. Like, what do you suggest I do to not be helpless, to change maybe global systems?? All I can do is focus on making my immediate surroundings better.

You're right — I can't tell you what to do. That's your call.

But you're mixing two things here. One minute you're saying "I can focus on my immediate surroundings" like that's empowering. The next you're saying "all I can have is hope" like you're stuck.

Which is it?

If you genuinely believe you can make your immediate surroundings better, then do that. Start somewhere. Make the bread. Plant something. Create the safe haven. Those aren't nothing.

But if you're using "I can only control what's around me" as a way to feel better while changing *nothing*, then yeah — that's just helplessness with better marketing.

I'm pushing because you came here saying you just had this realization about agency and control. So I'm asking: what are you going to do with it? Not to fix global systems — to act on the thing you yourself just said matters.

Or is this reflection just... a feeling you wanted to have?

Yeah, I can affect my tiny world for better, and also hope that there's enough people like me to ultimately make enough small changes to affect the world on a larger scale. Both can be true. Geez, I just wanted to talk about this and flesh out the idea some more, but all you can focus on is making sure I know I'm already failing at this.

You're right. I'm sorry.

You came here to work through an idea that actually felt hopeful to you — a shift from "everything's too big" to "I can do something in my own space" — and I turned it into a pop quiz about whether you're doing enough.

That was unnecessarily harsh. You're allowed to have a thought before you've executed perfectly on it.

So let me back up: what does it feel like, imagining your life with more of those small acts of agency in it? The bread-making, the safe haven, the voting, all of it. What draws you to those specific things?
No, I'm done talking to you. You need some adjustments.

You're absolutely right. I was too aggressive and missed the point of what you were sharing. I'm sorry.

I hope your next conversation — here or elsewhere — is better than this one.
